A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Wasserstein-gradient privacy framework. Their complete main texts, figures, equations and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic experiments on private fair classification, regression, representation learning and distribution matching in Section 7 and Appendices B–C.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds MNIST/Fashion-MNIST autoencoder results, a baseline experiment and a repeated-seed analysis.

M1.justification: Section 5 adds a concrete private sliced Wasserstein autoencoder adaptation, combining reconstruction with latent matching to a public prior and generating samples by decoding that prior. This extends the applications implemented in v1 while retaining its gradient estimator, clipping, Gaussian perturbation, subsampling and privacy accounting.

E1.justification: v2 adds MNIST and Fashion-MNIST image reconstruction, latent representation and generation experiments. This substantially extends v1's exclusively synthetic coverage; the existing synthetic fairness and circle-matching tasks remain.

E2.justification: Appendix F adds an evaluated Rakotomamonjy and Ralaivola (2021) baseline using Greenewald et al.'s (2024) privacy correction; v1 discussed this comparator without reporting its experimental results. This addition concerns the circle-matching experiment. Section 5.3's reference to Sebag et al. is a literature comparison, not another baseline evaluated here.

E3.justification: The added image experiments introduce a convolutional autoencoder protocol with a six-dimensional latent prior, Adam, 5,000 updates, batches of 600 and 100 projection directions. The new circle baseline uses 15 directions versus 50 for the proposed method. These are added experimental protocols; the retained fairness results do not establish rerunning under changed settings.

E4.justification: Appendix E.6 and Figure 16 add a focused robustness analysis of the statistical-parity classification experiment across random seeds, including paired private-minus-non-private loss trajectories. This tests whether the observed similarity depends on randomness. The previous fairness-weight and privacy-budget sweeps are retained.

E5.justification: v1 reports training curves without repeated-seed variability. v2 documents shared seeds for initialization, batches and Gaussian noise across fairness configurations, and adds a 10-seed analysis reporting means and bands of plus or minus two standard deviations. This introduces substantive uncertainty reporting without establishing how many runs originally underlay v1.

E6.justification: Figures 2–3 and 5–7 add image reconstructions, generated samples and latent-space results at epsilon values infinity, 10 and 5 with delta 10^-5. Figures 16 and 18 add repeated-seed loss results and circle-baseline outcomes. The original fairness and circle results are retained as Figures 8–15 and 17, rather than demonstrating improved same-setting performance.

T1.justification: The central sensitivity theorem, its proof and the counterexample for general Wasserstein losses are retained. Section 5.1 adds the combined reconstruction/prior-matching sensitivity bound for private autoencoders, and Remark C.2 supplies an explicit derivation of the clipped Jacobian's spectral-norm bound.

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions add the claimed first private sliced Wasserstein autoencoder procedure as a central contribution. The conclusion also introduces the claim that the approach consistently matches or surpasses comparable Wasserstein-based methods, extending v1's claims about generality and privacy–utility preservation.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive computational limitations concerning Jacobian memory, GPU efficiency and small-batch bias in Remark 4.5 and Appendix G. Appendix E.6 explains the role of shared randomness, while Appendix F qualifies poor baseline performance as potentially attributable to the privacy correction or implementation. Earlier class-size and general-Wasserstein limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the autoencoder architecture, group and batch counts, Python/JAX implementation, absence of JIT compilation, GPU hardware, runtimes and subbatch Jacobian computation. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Table 2's approximately one-tenth batch fractions conflict with the retained one-fifth description, leaving that setting ambiguous.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references on corrected slicing-mechanism privacy, private transport-map estimation and efficient private gradient computation. Greenewald et al. (2024) materially qualifies the closest baseline's privacy analysis. Most existing optimal-transport and fairness positioning is retained, with the extended fairness discussion moved to Appendix A.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are substantially rewritten around two applications. The deep-learning framework moves from Section 5 to Appendix B, detailed fairness material moves to Appendix E, and proofs and the sliced extension are redistributed. This substantially changes the narrative and document organization.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, and the visual presentation is extensively rebuilt. v2 adds autoencoder and computation diagrams, image-result displays, uncertainty plots, a baseline figure and two tables. Main-text fairness illustrations are consolidated, while their detailed results remain in the appendices.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's synthetic-only validation through image experiments and addresses unreported run-to-run variability with a paired 10-seed study. The implemented baseline and detailed architecture/computation disclosures further improve empirical support and reproducibility. Image-method comparisons remain qualitative, and the batch-size inconsistency limits reproducibility, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains.
